label: Madonna of the Yarnwinder

claims.value: Novellara to Isabella d'Este, Florence, 3 April 1501
claims.statement: Fra Pietro da Novellara, Carmelite vicar general, wrote to Isabella d'Este from Florence on 3 April 1501, in answer to her letter of 27 March 1501; the Mantua State Archive files this letter under the Saint Anne cartoon.

claims.value: Novellara to Isabella d'Este, Florence, 14 April 1501: the small picture for Florimond Robertet
claims.statement: Novellara's letter of 14 April 1501 reports that Leonardo was painting a small picture for Florimond Robertet, secretary of the King of France, showing the Madonna with a yarnwinder; the Mantua State Archive publishes a transcription (Archivio Gonzaga, b. 1103 per the archive's transcription file, to confirm).

claims.value: Two principal versions survive: Buccleuch and Lansdowne
claims.statement: Two principal versions survive: the Buccleuch Madonna (Duke of Buccleuch collection, on loan to the Scottish National Gallery, Edinburgh) and the Lansdowne Madonna (private collection, on loan to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York). Both share an underdrawing according to technical study.

sources.cite: Louvre, Leonardo exhibition 2019, mini site page on the Yarnwinder.
Wikipedia, Madonna of the Yarnwinder, background only, not grounds.

claims.value: Neither surviving version is securely the Robertet picture
claims.statement: Which (if either) of the surviving versions corresponds to the picture described in 1501 is a scholarly reconstruction; one view (reported in Wikipedia) takes the Buccleuch as the picture delivered to Robertet in 1507; The Art Newspaper reports another destination (Blois).

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Madonna of the Yarnwinder, background only, not grounds.
